newsitem.title: USA: Advanced Micro profits lower than expected.
newsitem.headline: Advanced Micro profits lower than expected.

text.p: Advanced Micro Devices Inc. on Tuesday reported second-quarter profits that were only a third of what Wall Street expected, reflecting slow sales of some of the company's older computer chips.

Like its bigger rival Intel Corp., Advanced Micro Devices -- better known as AMD -- is suffering a tough product transition. In April, AMD introduced the state-of-the-art K6 microprocessor, which has been selling well. But the K6 obliterated demand for the slower K5 chip, forcing prices lower, the company said.

AMD, based in Sunnyvale, California, earned $9.97 million, or 7 cents a share, compared with a loss of $34.67 million, or 26 cents, in the same quarter a year ago. Revenue for the quarter ended June 29 rose 31 percent to $594.6 milllion from $455.1 million a year ago.
Wall Street had expected AMD to earn 22 cents a share, according to a recent survey by the First Call service, which tracks analyst forecasts.
AMD released its results after the market closed. Its stock had closed up $1.125 at $39.125 for the day, but slid to as low as $36.625 in after-hours trading.

AMD makes microprocessors, the chips that are the heart of a computer. This quarter was closely watched by investors because of the K6 introduction. The chip -- which works about as fast as Intel's top-of-the-line Pentium chips but costs 25 percent less -- is expected to generate lots of revenue for AMD, but it killed sales of the company's K5 product lines.
Intel said in May it also expects weak second-quarter results. Its new Pentium II and Pentium MMX chips are eating into sales of older Pentium chips, Intel has said.

AMD said it sold $100 million worth of K6 chips since the April introduction, driving sales at its computation products group up 36 percent from the first quarter. It has shipped 350,000 K6 chips to date, the company said.

AMD also makes specialised logic, communications and flash memory chips. It also suffered because sales from those products, which account for two-thirds of total revenue, were "essentially flat" compared with the first quarter, AMD said.

Still, AMD executives told analysts during the conference call that they remain bullish for prospects until the end of the year. They said they expect to sell at least 1 million K6s in the third quarter.
"If you believe their numbers, their prospects are good," said David Wu, analyst at investment bank ABN AMRO Chicago Corp. "The reason for buying AMD's stock is the K6."
For the first half, AMD had net income of $22.9 million, or 16 cents a share, compared with a loss of $9.35 million, or 7 cents, in the same period a year ago.
Six-month revenues rose 15 percent to $1.15 billion from $999.3 million a year ago.
